article.title: Simpson’s Paradox: When Every Segment Says One Thing but the Total Says the Opposite
article.why: Deep Dive on aggregation, confounding, weighting, and causal interpretation.

paragraphs.en:
Business dashboards encourage aggregation. Executives want one conversion rate, one average spend figure, or one success rate that summarizes the whole organization. Aggregation is often necessary, but it can produce a striking statistical phenomenon: a trend that appears within several groups can weaken, disappear, or even reverse when those groups are combined. This is commonly associated with Simpson's paradox.

Consider two marketing channels, Search and Social, and two customer segments, Existing and New. Campaign A might outperform Campaign B among Existing customers and also outperform it among New customers. Yet Campaign B could show the higher conversion rate overall. The apparent contradiction is possible when the campaigns receive very different proportions of traffic from the two segments. If Existing customers convert easily and Campaign B receives mostly Existing customers, its aggregate rate can be high even though it performs worse within each comparable segment.

The arithmetic is driven by weighting. An overall conversion rate is a weighted average of segment-level rates, where the weights depend on how many observations fall into each segment. When the weights differ substantially between the groups being compared, the aggregate comparison reflects two things at once: performance within segments and differences in segment composition. If composition is strongly related to the outcome, it can dominate the total.

This matters far beyond marketing. A hospital treating more severe cases may have a worse overall mortality rate even if its outcomes are better within each severity category. A university may show a different overall admission pattern because applicants distribute themselves unevenly across departments with different acceptance rates. A retailer's total year-over-year growth may look weak because sales shifted toward a slow-growing region, even while every region improved relative to its own baseline.

The paradox is not a command to always trust segmented results over aggregate results. The appropriate comparison depends on the question. If management asks, 'What happened to the company-wide conversion rate?' the aggregate figure is a real descriptive fact. If the question is, 'Which campaign performs better for comparable customers?' then differences in customer composition may need to be controlled. Statistical adjustment is not about choosing the number we prefer; it is about aligning the comparison with the estimand—the quantity we actually want to learn.

Confounding is often central. A variable can influence both which group an observation enters and the outcome being measured. In the campaign example, customer status may affect channel or campaign exposure and also conversion propensity. Simply comparing aggregate conversion rates can therefore mix treatment effects with pre-existing differences. Randomization helps by making treatment assignment independent of such characteristics on average, although chance imbalance, noncompliance, attrition, and post-treatment selection can still complicate interpretation.

Analysts should also be careful about which variables they condition on. Segmenting by a genuine pre-treatment confounder can clarify a comparison, but controlling for a variable caused by the treatment can introduce new bias. For example, if a campaign changes website engagement and engagement then affects purchase, conditioning on engagement may block part of the effect we are trying to measure. Causal diagrams and a clear temporal understanding of variables are often more useful than mechanically adding every available field to a model.

A practical workflow begins by inspecting both aggregate and segmented results. Identify variables that strongly predict the outcome and whose distributions differ across comparison groups. Examine the weights behind the total. Then ask whether the goal is descriptive, predictive, or causal. For descriptive reporting, show the composition change explicitly. For predictive work, evaluate performance across relevant subpopulations. For causal questions, use a design or adjustment strategy justified by assumptions about how treatment, confounders, mediators, and outcomes relate.

Standardization can make comparisons easier to interpret. Instead of allowing Campaign A and Campaign B to retain their own customer mixes, an analyst can calculate what each campaign's conversion rate would be under a common reference distribution of Existing and New customers. This separates within-segment performance from composition. Regression, inverse probability weighting, stratification, and experimental designs offer related tools, but each relies on assumptions that should be stated rather than hidden behind technical sophistication.

Simpson's paradox is memorable because the reversal feels impossible at first. Its broader lesson, however, is ordinary and practical: totals inherit the weights of the populations that created them. Whenever two totals are compared, we are implicitly comparing both outcomes and composition. Before declaring that one campaign, store, hospital, model, or year is better than another, inspect who or what is inside each total, decide which comparison answers the business question, and make the weighting logic visible.

translations.zh:
擴充翻譯：Simpson’s paradox 指的是各 segment 內都呈現同一方向的差異，但合併後的總體結果可能減弱、消失，甚至反轉。關鍵在 weighting：總體 conversion rate 是各 segment rate 的加權平均，而不同比較組若擁有完全不同的 segment 組成，aggregate result 同時混合了「segment 內表現」與「composition 差異」。

因此不能簡單規定『永遠相信分群結果』。若問題是全公司 conversion rate 發生什麼變化，aggregate rate 本身就是有效的描述；若問題是 comparable customers 下哪個 campaign 表現較好，就需要控制 composition。這裡真正要對齊的是 estimand，也就是我們究竟想估計哪一個量。

Confounding 會讓問題更複雜：某變數若同時影響 exposure/treatment 與 outcome，單純比較總體結果就可能把 treatment effect 與既有差異混在一起。Randomization 可在平均意義下改善這個問題，但 attrition、noncompliance 或 post-treatment selection 仍可能破壞解讀。

實務流程是同時看 aggregate 與 segment results，檢查 outcome predictor 與各組 composition，理解總體數字背後的 weights，再區分問題是 descriptive、predictive 還是 causal。必要時可用 standardization，把不同組套到同一 reference distribution 上比較。Regression、IPW、stratification 等也能處理相關問題，但都依賴假設，不能只因技術複雜就視為自動正確。
translations.ja:
拡張訳：Simpson's paradoxでは、各segment内では同じ方向の差が見えていても、集計すると差が弱まったり、消えたり、逆転したりする。原因はweightingである。全体conversion rateはsegment別rateの加重平均であり、比較するgroup間でsegment構成が違えば、全体値には『segment内のperformance』と『構成比の差』が同時に入る。

ただし、常にsegment別結果の方が正しいわけではない。全社conversion rateそのものを知りたいならaggregate値は有効な記述である。一方、同等の顧客条件でcampaignを比較したいならcompositionを調整する必要がある。重要なのは、分析対象であるestimandと比較方法を一致させること。

またconfoundingにも注意する。treatment/exposureとoutcomeの両方に関係する変数があれば、単純なaggregate比較は効果と既存差を混同し得る。randomizationは有効だが、attritionやpost-treatment selectionなどで解釈が難しくなる場合もある。

実務ではaggregateとsegmentの両方を確認し、各groupの構成比とweightを可視化する。その上でdescriptive、predictive、causalのどの問いかを明確にする。必要なら共通のreference distributionを使うstandardizationなどで構成差を切り離す。高度な手法を使う場合も、その前提条件を明示することが重要である。

vocabulary.usage: Aggregation can hide differences in segment composition.
The paradox appears when aggregated and segmented trends point in opposite directions.
Customer composition affects the weights in an overall conversion rate.
Weighting determines how segment rates contribute to the total.
The estimand defines the quantity the analysis is intended to learn.
Confounding mixes treatment effects with pre-existing differences.
Attrition after randomization can complicate causal interpretation.
Noncompliance occurs when assigned treatment is not actually followed.
Conditioning on a mediator may block part of a treatment effect.
Standardization compares groups under a common reference distribution.
Stratification compares outcomes within defined covariate groups.
Inverse probability weighting uses probability-based weights for adjustment.
Comparing totals implicitly compares their population compositions.
Pre-existing differences can be mistaken for treatment effects.

business.term: Show both the aggregate result and the segment weights that produced it.
business.explanation: 同時呈現 aggregate 結果與形成它的 segment weights。

business.term: Align the comparison with the estimand rather than choosing the most favorable view.
business.explanation: 比較方法要對齊 estimand，而不是挑選最好看的結果。

business.term: Separate composition effects from within-segment performance.
business.explanation: 把 composition effect 與 segment 內表現拆開。

sources: Background: Simpson's paradox, weighted averages, confounding, standardization, causal inference, and stratified analysis.
